newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr sags as Japan worries return.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr sags as Japan worries return.

text.p: The Australian dollar was back under pressure late Wednesday due to a sudden flare-up in long running concerns over the health of Japanese investor demand.

The currency had steadied at 78 cents in the morning as talk of a domestic rate cut went off the boil, but was then dumped to US$0.7770 support by offshore players. Traders said the latest scare sprang from a Japanese newspaper report that Japanese investors were shifting funds from A$ bonds to U.S. assets.
"People have been afraid this would happen ever since the last RBA rate cut, so the report fits its prejudices," said one. "The market's in the mood to sell and this suits it well."
By 4.45 pm (0545 GMT) the local dollar had subsided to US$0.7777/83 from an early US$0.7803/08, to stand little changed from Tuesday's weak US$0.7778/84 finish.
The currency had looked to have won a breathing space from bear attentions this morning when speculation of an imminent rate cut was again scotched by Reserve Bank silence.

Dealers said with half the month gone even the most rabid rumourmonger was finding it hard to sustain the easing talk and most accepted that policy would not be changing before the next RBA board meeting on February 4. But a couple of weeks grace was not enough to prevent a wobble when the Japanese talk surfaced.

Traders said the newspaper report just echoed what many local players had been thinking since the RBA surprised markets with its December 11 rate cut. This made 150 basis points of easing in less than six months and sharply narrowed the premium offered by A$ paper over competing US$ bonds.
The market had also started to price in another cut in rates here, further reducing the gap and fuelling speculation the yield would no longer be attractive to Japanese investors.
The feeling was reinforced by a sharp slowing in the flow of yen/A$ dual currency issues which had been all the rage amongst Japanese retail investors last year.

Analysts emphasised that a Japanese bail out was far from a foregone conclusion given that Q4 consumer price data later this month should confirm that Australian inflation was running well below that in the U.S. and thus real A$ yields were still high.
Neither was a another RBA cut a certainty with some analysts expecting the bank to wait and see what effect the last three have had first.

The yen also had its own troubles as a sluggish Japanese economy was likely to keep rates there at record lows for months to come while positive U.S. fundamentals had propelled US$/yen into a strong uptrend, with benefits for all the dollar bloc.
Thus when the U.S. dollar jumped to a fresh 45-month high of 117.25 yen today, the local currency was able to finish firmer at 90.93/03 yen from 90.55/65 late Tuesday.
In trade weighted terms the currency ended steady at 58.2.
Today's domestic data were largely ignored as they neither argued for nor against another policy easing.

Housing finance commitments fell 2.9 percent in November after a 5.1 percent drop in October, which was a disappointing performance given that rates had been cut at the start of the month. All the weakness was in refinancing, however, and excluding this total commitments were up 0.6 percent.
Analysts noted there was usually a long lag before the impact of rate cuts was felt on housing demand and policy had been eased again since November.

More timely was the Westpac consumer sentiment index for January which rose 4.1 percent to partly reverse an unexpectedly steep 6.7 percent fall in December. Westpac said the bounce reflected the impact of the surprise December rate cut, but consumers were still cautious over job prospects.
Employment data for December are due Thursday and some expect to see a weakening in the already slow labour market.
